'''''Nymphaea elegans''''', also known as the '''tropical royalblue waterlily''',<ref name = "U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service">U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service. (n.d.). Tropical Royalblue Waterlily. Retrieved July 13, 2023, from https://www.fws.gov/species/tropical-royalblue-waterlily-nymphaea-elegans</ref><ref>{{PLANTS|id=NYEL|taxon=Nymphaea elegans|accessdate=11 September 2016}}</ref> is a species of [[aquatic plant]]s in the family [[Nymphaeaceae]]. It is native to the United States (Louisiana, Florida and Texas), Mexico, and the Bahamas. It has been introduced to Colombia.<ref name = "POWO, 2023" /> Additionally, it has been reported to occur in Argentina.<ref name = "Tur, 2006">Tur, N. M. (2006). [https://www.hickenia.darwin.edu.ar/index.php/hickenia/article/download/52/49 "''Nymphaea elegans'' (Nymphaeaceae) nueva cita para la flora Argentina."] Hickenia, 3, 42-167.</ref>

==Description==
This species has unbranched rhizomes, which do not produce stolons. The petiole does not have any trichomes. The upper leaf surface is green, the submerged side of the leaf is purple.<ref name = "SEINet">''Nymphaea elegans'' Hook. (n.d.). SEINet. Retrieved July 13, 2023, from https://swbiodiversity.org/seinet/taxa/index.php?taxon=27921&clid=83</ref>

==Reproduction==
The fragrant flowers are [[protogynous]]. During the first day of flowering they are functionally female. In the following two days, they are functionally male.<ref name = "Schneider, 1982">Schneider, E. L. (1982). [https://www.academia.edu/download/56320525/0304-3770_2882_2990014-620180414-5858-lk8sck.pdf "Notes on the floral biology of ''Nymphaea elegans'' (Nymphaeaceae) in Texas."] Aquatic Botany, 12, 197-200.</ref>

==Taxonomy==
===Type specimen===
The type specimen was collected from a pond near the head of Leona River in 1849 by [[Charles Wright (botanist)|Charles Wright]] in Texas, USA.<ref name = "Schneider, 1982" /><ref name = "IPNI, 2023">''Nymphaea elegans'' | International Plant Names Index. (n.d.). Retrieved July 13, 2023, from https://www.ipni.org/n/171178-2</ref>

==Etymology==
The specific epithet ''elegans'' means fine, elegant, or handsome.{{cn|date=July 2023}}

==Ecology==
===Herbivory===
[[File:Sandhill Crane JCB.jpg|thumb|right|''Nymphaea elegans'' is a food source of sandhill cranes in Texas, USA<ref name = "Guthery, 1975" />]]
''Nymphaea elegans'' has been reported to be an important food plant of [[sandhill crane]]s in Texas, USA. It makes up 8.7% of their diet's volume.<ref name = "Guthery, 1975">Guthery, F. S. (1975). Food Habits of Sandhill Cranes in Southern Texas. The Journal of Wildlife Management, 39(1), 221–223. https://doi.org/10.2307/3800493</ref>

==Uses==
It finds use as a medicine and for food.<ref name = "POWO, 2023" />
